prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Pavement slipp’ry, people sneezing, Lords in ermine, beggars freezing; Titled gluttons dainties carving, Genius in a garret starving. Lofty mansions, warm and spacious; Courtiers cringing and voracious; Misers scarce the wretched heeding; Gallant soldiers fighting, bleeding. Wives who laugh at passive spouses; Theatres, and meeting-houses; Balls, where simp’ring misses languish; Hospitals, and groans of anguish. Arts and sciences bewailing; Commerce drooping, credit failing; Placemen mocking subjects loyal; Separations, weddings royal. Authors who can’t earn a dinner; Many a subtle rogue a winner; Fugitives for shelter seeking; Misers hoarding, tradesmen breaking. Taste and talents quite deserted; All the laws of truth perverted; Arrogance o’er merit soaring; Merit silently deploring. Ladies gambling night and morning; Fools the works of genius scorning; Ancient dames for girls mistaken, Youthful damsels quite forsaken. Some in luxury delighting; More in talking than in fighting; Lovers old, and beaux decrepid; Lordlings empty and insipid. Poets, painters, and musicians; Lawyers, doctors, politicians: Pamphlets, newspapers, and odes, Seeking fame by diff’rent roads. Gallant souls with empty purses; Gen’rals only fit for nurses; School-boys, smit with martial spirit, Taking place of vet’ran merit. Honest men who can’t get places, Knaves who shew unblushing faces; Ruin hasten’d, peace retarded; Candor spurn’d, and art rewarded.

outputs.L2:
Slick footpaths and coughing crowds; nobility draped in fine fur while the poor shiver in the cold. The wealthy and titled slice up their delicacies, while brilliant minds go hungry in their attic rooms.

Grand houses, roomy and heated; fawning, greedy attendants at court; misers who barely notice the suffering around them; brave soldiers wounded in battle.

Women who mock their submissive husbands; playhouses and places of worship; dances where affected young ladies grow faint; hospitals echoing with cries of pain.

The arts and sciences in mourning; trade declining and financial trust collapsing; officeholders ridiculing faithful citizens; couples parting and royals marrying.

Writers unable to afford a meal; countless cunning cheats coming out ahead; those on the run searching for refuge; the greedy piling up wealth while merchants go bankrupt.

Good taste and ability abandoned; every principle of honesty twisted; pride rising above worthiness, while true worth grieves in silence.

Fashionable women betting away their days and nights; foolish people dismissing works of true brilliance; older women taken for young girls, and young women left neglected.

Some reveling in extravagance; more given to chatter than to combat; aged suitors and worn-out dandies; petty lords who are hollow and dull.

Poets, artists, and composers; attorneys, physicians, and statesmen; leaflets, newspapers, and verses—all chasing renown by their separate paths.

Brave hearts with empty pockets; commanders good for nothing but a sickbed; schoolboys caught up in warlike dreams, pushing aside experienced worth.

Decent people who can find no position; scoundrels wearing shameless expressions; destruction sped along and peace held back; sincerity rejected while trickery is rewarded.
outputs.L3:
# A Society in Decay: Themes of Injustice and Moral Corruption

The poem presents a stark and unflinching portrait of a divided world, juxtaposing extreme wealth against abject poverty. On one side stand the privileged aristocrats and indulgent gluttons, surrounded by comfort and excess; on the other shiver freezing beggars and starving geniuses, their talents and humanity ignored. This deliberate contrast exposes the profound inequality that defines the society under scrutiny, where fortune and merit rarely align.

Beyond mere material disparity, the poem depicts a fundamentally corrupt social order. Here, deceitful rogues, cunning knaves, and self-interested officials rise to prosperity, thriving on manipulation and dishonesty. Meanwhile, those who conduct themselves with integrity find themselves cast aside, struggling in vain to secure even honest work. The moral logic of this world is inverted, rewarding vice and punishing virtue.

The decline extends across every sphere of human achievement. The poem laments the deterioration of the arts and sciences, the decay of commerce, the failure of credit, and the collapse of once-thriving tradesmen. What should be the pillars of a flourishing civilization instead crumble, signaling a broader cultural and economic exhaustion.

At the heart of this critique lies a condemnation of perverted truth and justice. In this distorted world, arrogance and empty pretension triumph, while genuine merit suffers quietly, unrecognized and unrewarded. Those most deserving of honor are precisely those who endure in silence, denied their rightful place.

Finally, the poem turns a mocking eye upon the frivolity and vanity of the upper classes. It parades before the reader a procession of absurd figures: ladies consumed by gambling, decrepit old men playing at love, and incompetent leaders wholly unfit for the positions they occupy. Through this satirical lens, the poem exposes the hollowness of a ruling elite that has abandoned substance for spectacle, leaving a society adrift under their misguided stewardship.
outputs.L4:
# The Anatomy of Injustice: A Satirical Portrait of Urban Society

This satirical poem operates through a technique of rapid accumulation, presenting the reader with a swift, almost breathless catalogue of vivid and contrasting images. Rather than developing a single sustained argument, the poet assembles a mosaic of urban life in which each fleeting scene captures a particular moral failing or social contradiction. The effect is deliberately overwhelming: the sheer volume of injustices piled one upon another mirrors the relentless, inescapable nature of the corruption the poet seeks to expose.

At the heart of the poem lies a series of pointed juxtapositions. Wealth is set against poverty, so that the glittering excess of the few is thrown into sharp relief against the desperate want of the many. Virtue is measured against vice, and the poet takes particular delight in showing how frequently the two trade their expected fortunes—the good man languishing while the scoundrel flourishes. Merit, too, is contrasted with corruption, revealing a world in which genuine talent and integrity count for nothing against the currency of flattery, deceit, and connection.

The images the poet selects are chosen for their emotional and moral resonance. We encounter the starving genius, whose brilliance goes unrewarded and unrecognized, wasting away in obscurity while lesser minds prosper. We see the knave elevated and celebrated, gaining honours and riches he has done nothing to deserve. And we witness the honest man cast aside and neglected, his virtue treated not as an asset but as a liability in a society that has inverted its own values.

Through this relentless procession of contradictions, the poem builds toward a scathing indictment. Its ultimate target is a social order in which true worth is systematically ignored, while arrogance, dishonesty, and shameless self-promotion are rewarded with success. The cumulative force of the poem's imagery leaves the reader with an unmistakable impression of moral outrage—a sense that the world it depicts is not merely flawed but fundamentally, perversely upside down. In this way, the satire transcends simple complaint and becomes a broader condemnation of the hypocrisy and injustice that the poet sees corroding the very fabric of urban life.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Names

The rain-slicked **pavement** gleamed beneath the gas lamps as the carriages rolled past, their wheels splashing muddy water toward the doorways of London's oldest establishments. On these ancient stones, generations had walked—merchants and beggars, poets and thieves—but tonight the street belonged to a different kind of traveler.

Inside the grand hall, the **Lords** gathered as they had for centuries. Robed in ermine and crimson, they filled the benches with the murmur of privilege and power. Each man carried a legacy older than the building itself, their voices shaping laws that would echo across the empire. Here, decisions were made that never touched the wet cobblestones outside, yet somehow determined the fate of every soul who walked them.

Among the assembly sat the newly **titled** baron, a man who only months before had been a commoner. He fidgeted with the unfamiliar weight of his robes, acutely aware of how strange it felt to be called *"my lord."* His journey from the humble streets to these gilded chambers had been swift and improbable—a fortune made, a favor granted, a name suddenly elevated above the crowd.

As the session ended, he stepped back onto that same **pavement** where he had once hurried as a nobody. The stones had not changed. The rain fell the same as ever. But the world now regarded him differently, and he wondered whether a title could truly transform a man, or whether it merely dressed him in borrowed importance.

The **Lords** dispersed into the night, their carriages carrying them home, while the pavement—patient and indifferent—waited for the morning crowds to return.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical poem in rhyming couplets describing the contradictions and social ills of city life, listing scenes of wealth beside poverty, corruption beside virtue.
counterfactuals.output:
# The City's Ledger

Behold the city, grand and gleaming bright,
Where golden towers scrape the smoggy night,
While in their shadows, huddled on the stone,
The beggar counts his coppers, all alone.

The banker rides his chauffeured limousine
Past children hawking papers, gaunt and lean;
He signs a check to charity with pride,
Then evicts the tenants living just outside.

The senator, so eloquent and fair,
Decries corruption with a righteous air,
Yet pockets bribes in envelopes discreet,
And feasts on lobbyists' expensive meat.

A saint distributes bread to those in need,
While merchants prosper on the sin of greed;
The preacher thunders "virtue!" from his pew,
Then slips away to sample something new.

Here Fashion struts in furs and diamond rings,
While Hunger scavenges through rotting things;
The gourmet sends his lobster back, too cold,
As orphans dream of crusts a day too old.

The judge who sentences the petty thief
Accepts his "gifts" and grants the rich relief;
Justice is blind, we're told with solemn nod—
Blind to the poor, but winks at those with wad.

The influencer sells her soul online
For likes and sponsors, calling ruin "fine,"
While honest laborers, ignored, unseen,
Keep turning wheels of this vast, thankless machine.

O city of contradictions, gilded, cursed,
Where best and worst are tangled, blessed and worst!
You promise all, yet keep the game unfair—
A paradise for some, a wolf's den's lair.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of 18th-century English verse that paints a panoramic picture of London society, its vices, and injustices.
counterfactuals.output:
# London Survey'd

_A Poem in the Manner of the Age_

Where Thames, dark-flowing, laves the crowded shore,
And bears his freight of Commerce, Vice, and War,
There LONDON spreads her many-gilded pride,
And hides in splendour all she cannot hide.
Come, gentle Muse, forsake th' Arcadian grove,
Nor sing of shepherds, nor of trifling Love;
But turn thy pencil to a sterner scene,
And paint the City's glory—and her spleen.

Behold, at dawn, the labouring wretch arise,
Ere Fashion wakes, or Fortune rubs her eyes:
He treads the pavement worn with honest feet,
And begs a farthing in the frozen street;
While o'er his head, in chariots warm and vast,
The pamper'd Peer goes thundering swiftly past,
Nor casts a glance, nor stays the gilded wheel,
To mark what pangs the shivering poor may feel.

Here Justice sits, with balance held on high,
Yet weighs the purse before she weighs the cry;
The rich man's crime a lenient statute meets,
The pauper hangs for bread he stole to eat.
See Tyburn's tree its fatal branches spread,
Where Want, not Malice, bows the guilty head!
The Judge, well-fed, pronounces solemn doom,
Then dines on venison in his panell'd room.

In gaudy halls, where painted Vice presides,
And Folly's tide o'er squander'd fortune glides,
The Gamester trembles at the fickle die,
And stakes his acres with a frantic eye.
There Luxury, in silks of Eastern loom,
Perfumes the air, and hastens to the tomb;
While Flattery bends, and courts the vacant great,
And smiling Ruin waits upon their state.

The Poet starves, though genius fire his line;
The Quack grows rich, and rides in coach-and-nine.
The Statesman barters honour for a place,
And wears his falsehood with a courtier's grace;
The Bishop, mitred, shuns the sacred cause,
And loves his prebend better than his laws.
Even holy Charity, that seem'd so fair,
Is but a name to grace the wealthy heir.

At midnight now, along the reeling town,
The drunkard staggers, and the doors fall down;
From reeking cellars, Gin's blue vapours rise,
And Mothers pledge their infants for supplies.
Disease and Murder prowl the narrow lane,
And Law walks blindfold through the dark domain;
The watchman nods; the thief pursues his trade;
And Innocence is bought, and Virtue's sold.

Yet not all dark: amid this teeming maze,
Some steady lamps of honest Merit blaze—
The tradesman just, the matron chaste and mild,
The father toiling for his ragged child;
These, though obscure, a nobler triumph own
Than all the pageants of the gilded throne.
For Heaven, that marks the sparrow when it dies,
Beholds the lowly with unclouded eyes.

Then hear, O City, whom thy vices stain,
Nor let the Muse have sung her strains in vain:
Not marble domes, nor Commerce ranging wide,
Can prop a nation swoln with selfish pride.
When Justice sleeps, and Mercy quits her seat,
The proudest Empire moulders to defeat;
But Virtue, cherish'd, bids a people stand,
And spreads her guardian ægis o'er the land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a long list-style poem cataloging the follies of high society—gambling ladies, starving geniuses, cringing courtiers, and idle aristocrats?
counterfactuals.output:
The Vanity Fair: A Catalogue of Follies

**I. The Gambling Ladies**

Behold the Duchess at her cards,
Who stakes her jewels, her lands, her name,
Who wagers what she cannot lose
And loses more than gold—her fame;

The Countess with her trembling hands,
Who prays to dice as others pray,
Who mortgages tomorrow's bread
To feed the hunger of today;

Lady Vane, whose midnight losses
Would clothe a hundred shivering poor,
Yet weeps not for the beggar's crust
But for the ace behind the door.

**II. The Starving Geniuses**

The poet in his garret cold,
Whose verses shame the age's kings,
Yet dines on nothing but his pride
And warms his hands on what he sings;

The painter of immortal light
Who cannot buy a single candle,
Whose canvas holds the very sun
Yet whose own hearth's too poor to handle;

The philosopher whose thought
Could reorder half the earth,
Reduced to counting empty coins
And measuring his mind's true worth—

While patrons pass with powdered wigs,
Too busy praising last year's dead
To notice living greatness kneel
And beg a shilling for its bread.

**III. The Cringing Courtiers**

The flatterer with supple spine,
Who bends before he's even asked,
Whose every word is honeyed lie,
Whose true self hides behind a mask;

The bower and the scraper both,
Who trade their honor for a glance,
Who'd sell their mothers, sell their souls,
To join the sovereign's evening dance;

The whisperer at every ear,
The carrier of poisoned tales,
Who rises as his betters fall,
Whose only compass points where power sails;

The yes-man in his velvet coat,
Who's never spoken his own mind,
So long has he agreed with all
He's quite forgotten he had a spine.

**IV. The Idle Aristocrats**

The lord who's never turned a hand
Save lifting glasses to his lips,
Whose greatest labor is to yawn,
Whose deepest thought is how it slips—

The heir who counts his ancient blood
As if it were a great achievement,
Who did no more to earn his rank
Than draw first breath—a mere bereavement

Of any purpose, any use,
He drifts through gilded, echoing halls,
A portrait that has learned to walk,
A shadow leaning on the walls;

The lady who has never known
What hour the sun consents to rise,
Who thinks the world begins at noon
And ends where her own mirror lies;

The young blood racing phaetons
Through streets where working men must scatter,
Who'd weep more for a broken wheel
Than for the child his wheels might shatter.

**V. The Whole Menagerie**

And so they turn, this brilliant wheel,
This carousel of painted pride,
The gambler and the flatterer,
The genius starved, the fop supplied;

They dance their minuet of waste
While Time, the only honest guest,
Stands quiet by the ballroom door
And marks them each for his arrest;

For all their silks and all their airs,
Their titles carved in ancient stone,
They'll bow at last to that grave lord
Who levels palace, hut, and throne—

And there the Duchess and her maid,
The poet and the powdered peer,
Shall share one silence, share one dust,
And none shall know who once was here.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a witty period poem contrasting the rich and poor, using short rhyming couplets to satirize politics, arts, war, and fashion.
counterfactuals.output:
**Of Coin and Kind: A Satyr in Couplets**

*In the manner of the Age of Reason*

---

**I. Of Politics**

The rich man votes, and buys the votes of ten;
The poor man votes—then sells his voice again.
The Statesman swears he serves the common good;
He'd serve it better boiled, and richly stewed.
A promise, cheap, is coin that Parliaments dispense—
They pay in pledges, and they keep the pence.

**II. Of Arts**

The Patron yawns before a marbled Muse,
And buys the Painter what the Painter chews.
The starving Poet pens a lord's renown,
Then dies of Genius in a garret gown.
Thus Fame's a feast where none but flatterers dine—
The Artist furnishes; the rich recline.

**III. Of War**

The General plots his glory o'er the map;
The peasant's son shall plug the fatal gap.
One earns a medal broad as any moon;
One earns a grave, and earns it rather soon.
The rich lament the War with claret sighs—
The poor lament it less: the poor are *why.*

**IV. Of Fashion**

Her Ladyship wears feathers, France, and lace;
The scullery wears soot upon her face.
A wig may cost what feeds a street a year—
The louse, at least, is democratic here.
For Powder, Silk, and Ribbon rule the town,
While Honesty goes threadbare, patched, and brown.

---

**Envoi**

So spins the world: the great man dines on Praise,
The small man dines on Nothing, all his days.
Yet mark this jest the tomb shall shortly tell—
The Duke and Ditcher rot alike, and *well.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write "A Picture of the Times" as a satirical poem in the manner of Georgian-era social commentary.
counterfactuals.output:
# A Picture of the Times

*In heroic couplets, after the manner of the Age*

Come, gentle Muse, and lend thy candid eye
To paint the Town, its follies, and its lie;
Where Virtue wears a mask at every ball,
And Honour's cheapest at the auction-stall.

Behold the Beau, who spends the livelong day
In studious thought—of nothing but his stay;
Whose learning lies within his tailor's book,
Whose deepest reading is the looking-glass's look.
He courts the ladies with a practised sigh,
And borrows sentiment he cannot buy.

See yonder Statesman, honest as the rest,
Who wears the Nation's welfare in his breast—
So near the pocket that the two combine,
And what he calls his Country proves his wine.
He votes for Liberty with liberal hand,
Then sells the selfsame Freedom of the land.

The Lady Fashion, delicate and pale,
Who faints at Virtue, but ne'er fails to fail,
Reads sermons wrapped about her powder-puff,
And thinks a blush sufficient moral stuff.
She weeps at plays, is charitable, kind—
To all but servants, husbands, and mankind.

The Parson dines where richest tables groan,
And loves his neighbour's mutton as his own;
He thunders Hell upon the pauper's head,
Then damns the poor for wanting daily bread.
His flock may starve—he counts it no great crime,
So long as tithes come punctual at their time.

O Age of Reason! Age of powder'd wit!
Where Sense is banished and where Cant must sit;
Where every vice hath learned a decent name,
And Impudence is christened noble Fame.
Yet still the Muse, though laughed at by the Town,
Shall write the Times—and write the Great Ones down.

*Finis*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
